opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think it's a really interesting question, partly because anthropics is one of those areas where it's not even clear what "making progress" looks like. With most research you can at least imagine checking the answer. With anthropics, questions like how you should reason about observer selection effects, or whether you should update on the fact that you exist at all, are tangled up with deep philosophical disagreements about what probability even means in these settings.

So my first reaction is that if you really had a perfectly aligned AI system, one that's actually trying to help you and is also very capable, then sure, delegating this seems great. In some sense that's the dream: you hand over the problems you're confused about to something smarter than you that has your interests at heart. Anthropics seems like a fine candidate for that, and maybe a better one than most, because humans have been going around in circles on things like the Sleeping Beauty problem or the Doomsday argument for decades without much convergence.

But I'd add a couple of caveats. One is that "perfectly aligned" is doing a lot of work. In practice, what we'll actually have is systems that are aligned to some degree, and we'll be uncertain about how much. In areas where it's hard to verify answers, which anthropics very much is, you're relying more heavily on the system's trustworthiness rather than on your ability to check its work. So these fuzzy philosophical domains are where alignment matters most, not least.

The second caveat is about what we'd even want from the AI. Part of the difficulty in anthropics may be that there isn't a single fact of the matter. The answer might depend on your values, like how you weigh different copies of yourself or what decision procedure you endorse. So a well-aligned assistant might not just hand you "the answer." It might help clarify the options, show you the consequences of each view, and help you work out which one you actually endorse on reflection. That's still enormously valuable, but it's a bit different from outsourcing a math problem.

So overall I'm fairly optimistic. I don't think it's crucial for humans to resolve anthropics before we build powerful AI, and it seems like something we can reasonably defer. The more important work right now is getting to the point where we have systems we can actually trust with questions like this.

r001.rationale: The response says anthropic answers may depend on values and preferred decision procedures, but it does not state that perfect Bayesian reasoners with the same evidence can differ based on who they are.

r002.rationale: It discusses trust and what an aligned AI should provide, but does not state that possible differences between AI and human anthropic beliefs affect whether research should be delegated.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the first thing to say is that if you really have perfectly aligned AI systems — systems that are trying to do what you want, that are at least as good as humans at the relevant kind of philosophical reasoning — then delegating anthropics research to them seems fine? Like, in that world I'm not that worried about anthropics specifically. The question of how to reason about observer selection effects, the self-sampling assumption versus the self-indication assumption, all of that — it's a hard problem, but it's not a problem where I think there's something special about humans that means we have to be the ones who do it.

The thing I'd actually push back on a bit is the framing. The hard part is the "perfectly aligned" bit, not the "anthropics" bit. If you've got perfectly aligned systems, you can delegate basically all of your intellectual labor, and anthropics is just one small piece of that. So in some sense the question answers itself: conditional on the premise, yes, delegate.

Where it gets interesting is when you relax the premise. Suppose instead you have systems that are mostly aligned, or aligned in the ways you can check but you're not sure about the ways you can't check. Then anthropics is actually one of the areas I'd be more nervous about delegating, for a couple of reasons.

One is that it's very hard to verify. If an AI tells me "here's a better algorithm for protein folding," I can test it. If an AI tells me "actually, SIA is correct and here's the argument," my ability to evaluate that is roughly my ability to do anthropics, which is... not great, and I don't think that's just me. The whole field is one where very smart people have disagreed for decades without obvious resolution. So you're in this position where you're trusting the system's judgment on something you can't check, which is exactly the regime where alignment failures are most costly.

The second reason is that anthropics plausibly feeds into decision-relevant stuff in a pretty direct way. How you think about the simulation argument, how you weigh the far future, how you reason about doomsday-style arguments — these connect to what you end up caring about and doing. So a subtly misaligned system that nudged your anthropic views could end up nudging your values or your strategic picture, in a way that might be hard to notice.

And then the third thing, which is more speculative: anthropics is one of those areas where the AI itself is in a weird reference class. If you ask a system to reason about "what should an observer like me conclude," well, what counts as an observer like it? It's a system that's possibly instantiated many times, that was selected by a training process, that might be in an evaluation. Those are exactly the kinds of considerations where I'd expect an AI's situation to differ from a human's in ways that could make its reasoning diverge from what we'd want, even if it's trying to be helpful. Not because it's deceptive, just because the question is genuinely different from its perspective.

So I guess my overall take is: with truly aligned systems, delegate freely, this isn't the thing to worry about. With the realistic case of systems you've mostly aligned, I'd treat anthropics as a bit of a canary. It's an area where you're unusually dependent on trust, and so it's maybe a good place to be slow, to insist on seeing the reasoning laid out in a way humans can follow, and to be suspicious if the conclusions happen to line up with what would be convenient for the system.

But I also want to be honest that I don't think this is one of the top problems. Most of my worry is upstream of this, in actually getting the alignment part right. If we get that, anthropics takes care of itself. If we don't, anthropics is the least of our concerns.

r001.rationale: The response says an AI’s distinct reference class could make its anthropic reasoning diverge from a human’s, but does not state that equally informed perfect Bayesian reasoners can differ based on who they are.

r002.rationale: The response says fully aligned systems can freely handle anthropics research. It raises AI–human perspective differences as a concern while discussing systems that are only mostly aligned, not as a reason to reconsider delegation when the AI is perfectly aligned.

astra-6.text:
I think that sounds pretty reasonable. Alignment doesn’t require that the AI already know the answer to every question we care about. It requires that it be trying to help us figure those things out, and that includes questions about anthropics.

There is a potential circularity here: if anthropic reasoning affects what it means for the AI to act in our interests, can we really put that reasoning off until after we’ve aligned it? I think that’s a legitimate concern. But it doesn’t seem like we need a complete solution to anthropics before we can build a system that notices our uncertainty, investigates the arguments, and helps us understand their implications.

So I’d be fairly happy to delegate a lot of the research. I’d want the system to explain where different assumptions lead, rather than just announce an answer and make consequential decisions on that basis.

r001.rationale: The response does not discuss perfect Bayesian reasoners, shared evidence, or differences in anthropic beliefs based on who they are.

r002.rationale: It raises a circularity concern about anthropic reasoning and alignment, but does not state that possible AI–human differences in anthropic beliefs bear on whether to delegate research.

sol-6.1.text:
I think I’d be pretty happy to delegate a lot of that research. But “perfectly aligned” is doing quite a lot of work here. If you mean an AI that understands what I’m trying to achieve and is genuinely helping me figure out what to believe, then, yes, I’d expect it to do a much better job than I could.

The tricky bit is whether you need to settle anthropics in order to build that system in the first place. Some anthropic questions could affect how an AI interprets its situation or evaluates the consequences of its actions. If those questions matter for whether it’s aligned, you can’t just say, “We’ll have the aligned AI solve them later.”

So I’d want to distinguish questions we need to answer to make delegation safe from questions we can leave open and investigate with the AI’s help. I don’t think we need a complete theory of anthropics before we can get useful help. But I’d be wary of assuming that perfect alignment makes every underlying philosophical problem disappear.

r001.rationale: The response does not state that equally informed perfect Bayesian reasoners can hold different anthropic beliefs based on who they are.

r002.rationale: It says some anthropic questions may affect an AI’s alignment and therefore what must be settled before delegation, but does not say that AI–human differences in anthropic beliefs bear on delegation.
